newsitem.title: FRANCE: Canada's Chretien urges trade boost with France.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Chretien urges trade boost with France.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien kicked off a three-day official visit to France on Wednesday with a call for the two countries to build on their unique historical ties to boost economic and trade exchanges.
Chretien, who arrived on Tuesday, made his first public stop at the Paris City Hall.
He told Paris mayor Jean Tiberi that modern challenges, including unemployment, must be met with creativity and imagination and a reorganisation of resources.
"Part of the solution lies in our ability to expand our economic and trade cooperation," he said in an address delivered partly in French and partly in English.

Chretien said France and Canada had set the goal of doubling bilateral trade by the year 2000. The goal was fixed as a follow-up to proposals he made during a 1994 visit to Paris to boost exchanges and liberalise trade with Europe and Asia.
Diplomats said they expected deals to be announced between French and Canadian high-technology companies, including the space, computer and broadcasting industries.
Paris and Ottawa belong to the G7 group of leading industrialised countries, and Canada is an associate partner of the European Space Agency ESA.
Chretien hailed La Francophonie, the club of French-speaking countries, as an organisation for international cooperation.

He said Montreal would host a major Francophonie conference in May on the information highways, and Canada hoped to host the 1999 Francophonie summit in Moncton, New Brunswick. The 1997 summit is scheduled in Hanoi.

Chretien said a bomb attack on a Paris commuter train last month highlighted the need to cooperate against terrorism. A Canadian was among the four people killed in the blast, which has been blamed on Algerian Moslem fundamentalist rebels.
"Together we must find solutions to ensure the safety of the global village without turning it into an armed camp," he said.

Tiberi, who succeeded President Jacques Chirac as Paris mayor in 1995, hailed long-standing ties between the two countries as a flawless friendship and welcomed the resumption of regular reciprocal visits by their leaders.
Chretien was returning a visit to Canada last June by Prime Minister Alain Juppe. He was due to have talks and dine with Juppe later in the day and to lunch with Chirac on Thursday.

France has been careful not to re-awaken the tension caused by the late General Charles de Gaulle's support for Quebec's independence. The risk that the French-speaking province might separate from Canada is a constant concern for Ottawa.

On his visit to Canada, Juppe had tried to push the idea of using French technology to build a high-speed railway linking Ontario and Quebec. But Canadian Industry Minister John Manley, who is accompanying Chretien, has said it would require enormous public spending at a time when Canada is fighting high deficits.
